---
title: "Grounding AI in real sources: what a retrieval tool fixes, and what it cannot"
subtitle: "AIM-1 · AIM-9 · about one hour"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Explain what a context window is, and why a chatbot's apparent memory of your
   conversation is the whole conversation being sent again every turn.
2. State plainly that a language model does not learn from you, and say what
   does change between one turn and the next.
3. Describe the retrieval pipeline in order: chunk, embed, index, retrieve,
   augment, generate, and say what chunking does to a results table.
4. Explain why a source-grounded tool fabricates citations at a structurally
   lower rate than a general chatbot, and why that is not the same as being more
   careful.
5. Catch the failure grounding does not fix: a real, correctly linked source
   that the summary has misread or over-generalized.
6. Build a grounded notebook from sources you chose, and say when that is and is
   not a literature search.
:::

**Time.** About 20 minutes of reading, 7 minutes of video, 30 minutes of doing.
You need a Google account for NotebookLM (personal is fine; see the access note
in the Do block) and one general-purpose chatbot in a second tab, such as your
institutional ChatGPT Edu or Microsoft Copilot. Nothing installs. NotebookLM's
free tier allows 50 sources per notebook and 50 questions a day
[VERIFY: limits taken from third-party guides, 2026-09; check Google's own help page before the cohort]{.verify},
which is more than this chapter needs, but do not spend the day's questions in the first ten minutes.

## Journal club is Thursday

You are three weeks into a sub-internship. The chief resident hands you a
paper to present at Thursday's journal club, and four more "for background,"
because the topic is whether retrieval-grounded AI tools are ready for the
clinic and she knows you have opinions. It is Monday. You have five PDFs, two
call shifts, and a personal statement to finish.

A co-intern says: drop them all into NotebookLM and ask it your questions. You
do. Ten seconds later you have this.

::: {.grounded-answer}
<div class="q">Did adding retrieval improve the accuracy of the language models on the guideline questions, and did it work for all the models?</div>
<div class="a">Adding guideline retrieval improved accuracy across all models, with a pooled gain of +0.64 points (95% CI 0.47–0.80) on the automated judge.<a class="cite" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/">1</a> The benefit was largest for weaker models, with Mistral, Qwen3, and GPT-OSS showing gains of +0.72 to +0.94 points, but modest or absent for already-strong models like DeepSeek and GPT-5.<a class="cite" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/">1</a> Additionally, hallucination rates plummeted from 42% to 4% consistently across all base models when retrieval was enabled.<a class="cite" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/">1</a></div>
<div class="srcs">1 · Vollmer et al., <i>Diagnostics</i> 2026 · Results, Table 6. Real output of a source-grounded summarizer on 2026-09-07; provenance in the "One real specimen" section below.</div>
:::

Every number in that answer is real. Every little blue "1" links to a passage
that exists. The first sentence is going on your slide, and the first sentence
is not what the paper says.

This chapter is about why the numbers are real, why the sentence is not, and
how to tell in under a minute. The appraisal chapter showed you that a general
chatbot invents references and a retrieval tool does not. This one goes a level
down, into the machinery, because the machinery is what tells you which
mistakes are still possible after the references are fixed.

## Why this matters

In residency you will read less than you do now and rely on summaries more.
Some of those summaries will come from tools like the one above: a grounded
tool inside the EHR that answers from your institution's protocols, a
literature tool that indexes PubMed, a notebook you built from a rotation's
reading list. The vendors will tell you, correctly, that these tools "cite
their sources." What they will not say is what "cite" means mechanically, and
therefore which errors citing protects you from and which it does not.

When a notebook misreads a paper, the cost is a wrong slide. When the
grounded tool inside the EHR misreads a protocol, the cost lands on a patient,
and the clinician who repeated the sentence owns it.

The second reason is smaller and closer. The same mechanism that makes a
grounded tool trustworthy about *where* a sentence came from tells you why a
chatbot has no memory, why nothing you type teaches it anything, and why
pasting a patient's note into a consumer tool is a data question and not a
learning question. Those three facts are the AIM-1 foundations most clinicians
get wrong in the same direction, and a single hour fixes them.

## The idea

### The model has no memory

Start with something you can see. Open a chatbot and ask it who won the 2020
World Series. It answers (the Dodgers). Ask "where was it played?" and it
answers correctly (Arlington, Texas, because of the pandemic). It seems to
remember the first question.

It does not. Here is what the model actually received on the second turn:

```
[user]      Who won the 2020 World Series?
[assistant] The Los Angeles Dodgers won the 2020 World Series ...
[user]      Where was it played?
```

The entire conversation is sent again, every turn, and the model produces the
next piece of text given all of it. That block of text is the **context
window**: everything the model can see at the moment it answers. It is measured
in **tokens**, words or pieces of words, and it has a fixed size. When you
close the tab, the context is gone and the model is exactly what it was before
you opened it.

Two consequences follow, and both are load-bearing for the rest of the
chapter.

First, a language model does not learn from its users. Nothing you type
changes the model's weights, the billions of numbers set during training that
make it what it is. What changes between turns is the context, and only the
context. "It got better as we talked" means "the context got longer," and a
new conversation starts from zero. The privacy question is a separate one: the
company may *store* what you type, and some free tiers use it to train the
*next* model months later. That is a data-handling problem, not the model
remembering you, and it is the reason for the no-patient-information rule in
every chapter of this course.

Second, the context window is a budget, and the model does not use all of it
equally. When researchers placed the one relevant document at different
positions among many, model accuracy was highest when it sat at the beginning
or end of the context and fell when it was in the middle, in some settings
below the model's accuracy with no documents at all
[@doi:10.1162/tacl_a_00638]. Long context is not the same as attention. That
matters for what comes next, because a retrieval tool's whole job is to decide
which few passages go into the window.

### What "grounded" means mechanically

The appraisal chapter's figure showed two roads to a citation: a general model
generates a reference as text, and a retrieval tool searches first and writes
second (see @fig-citation-paths in the appraisal chapter). The searching-first
road has six steps, and each one is a place where something can go wrong.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-rag-pipeline
%%| fig-cap: "The retrieval pipeline. The left column happens once, when you add a source. The right column happens every time you ask a question. Nothing in either column reads the paper the way you would."
flowchart LR
  subgraph I["When you add a source"]
    direction TB
    doc[Your PDF] --> chunk[1. Chunk: cut into passages of a few hundred words]
    chunk --> embed[2. Embed: turn each passage into a list of numbers]
    embed --> index[3. Index: store the numbers so similar ones are findable]
  end
  subgraph Q["When you ask a question"]
    direction TB
    q[Your question] --> retrieve[4. Retrieve: embed the question, find the nearest passages]
    retrieve --> augment[5. Augment: paste those passages into the context window]
    augment --> generate[6. Generate: write an answer, pointing at the passages]
  end
  index -.-> retrieve
```

**Chunking** cuts the document into passages, because a whole paper will not
fit in the context window alongside your question and forty other papers. A
typical passage is a few hundred to a thousand tokens; one published clinical
pipeline used 1,024-token chunks and reported 97.5% citation accuracy on
seminal spine-surgery papers [@pmid:40662770], and a dental-trauma tool built
from five guideline sources was a knowledge base of exactly 250 chunks
[@pmid:42546813]. Chunking is dumb by design. It cuts on length, not meaning.

**Embedding** turns each passage into a list of numbers, an **embedding**, in
which passages about similar things get similar numbers. "Apixaban reduced
major bleeding" and "less hemorrhage with the factor Xa inhibitor" land near
each other; "the patient's dog is named Apixaban" does not. This is the
machinery from the word-embeddings talk in Go deeper, and you do not need it
to go further than "similar meaning, nearby numbers."

**Indexing** stores those numbers so that, given a new list of numbers, the
nearest ones can be found in milliseconds. An **index** is a phonebook sorted
by meaning instead of by surname.

**Retrieval** embeds your question the same way and pulls the nearest few
passages, usually somewhere between three and twenty. **Augmentation** pastes
them into the context window, in front of your question, as text. Then
**generation** is the ordinary thing a language model does, produce plausible
next words, except that now the most plausible continuation of "according to
the passages above" is something the passages actually say, and a citation is
a pointer back to a passage that is sitting right there in the window.

That is the entire trick. The model did not become honest. It was handed the
answer and asked to paraphrase it.

### What chunking does to a table

Here is the step most explanations skip, and the one that produces the
strangest errors. Consider a results table in a paper you uploaded. It is a
few lines of text. If the chunk boundary falls inside it, the tool stores
this:

::: {.chunks}
<pre class="chunk"><span class="lbl">chunk 7 of 23</span>... rated by three blinded specialists.

Table 6. Judge accuracy by model, with and without retrieval (mean, 95% CI).

Model             Without   With    Difference
Mistral Small     3.40      4.34    +0.94 (0.58–1.30)
Qwen3-Next        3.52      4.38    +0.86 (0.50–1.22)</pre>
<pre class="chunk"><span class="lbl">chunk 8 of 23</span>GPT-OSS-120B      3.62      4.34    +0.72 (0.36–1.08)
DeepSeek-V3.2     4.08      4.44    +0.36 (−0.01–0.72)
GPT-5-chat        4.18      4.48    +0.30 (−0.07–0.66)

The gain was large for the weaker models and small and not statistically significant for the already-strong bases ...</pre>
:::

Chunk 8 has the rows that matter for the question in the opening scenario, and
chunk 8 has no column headings. When it is retrieved alone, the model sees
five numbers per line and has to guess what they mean. When only chunk 7 is
retrieved, the model sees the headings and the two best-behaved rows and never
sees the sentence that qualifies them. Both chunks are real. Both citations
will resolve. Neither is the table.

Nothing in the pipeline knows that a table is a table, that a figure legend
belongs to a figure, or that "not statistically significant" three lines later
modifies the number above it. Rows of a table that are cut apart, a footnote
separated from the value it qualifies, a "however" at the top of the next
page: these are the retrieval tool's characteristic errors, and they are
errors of *reading*, made on a source that is real.

### Why grounded tools fabricate less: the numbers

The appraisal chapter gave you the headline: on a 2/1/0 scale, a tool that
indexes PubMed produced no fabricated citations while general chatbots
fabricated between 2% and 26% [@pmid:42232526]. The mechanism above is why,
and the same pattern repeats wherever it has been measured.

When six models answered 50 questions from a head-and-neck oncology
guideline, with and without retrieval of that guideline, content-level
hallucination fell from 42% to 4% and the fraction of citations that pointed
at a real retrieved passage rose from 0% to between 51% and 89%, depending on
the model [@pmid:42587692]. In implant dentistry, two retrieval systems
answered with 0% fabricated references while a general model fabricated 82%
of its references and 86% of its statistics [@pmid:41266194]. A 2026
systematic review of 44 studies found retrieval the most frequently tested
mitigation and reported 30% to 50% reductions in hallucination from it alone
[@pmid:42251377].

![What retrieval changes, and by how much. Six language models answered 50
questions from a clinical guideline, with and without retrieval of that
guideline. Redrawn from the reported figures in Vollmer et al., *Diagnostics*
2026 (open access, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)).
The groundedness bar shows the range across models.](../images/retrieval-hallucination-vollmer-2026.svg){#fig-vollmer fig-alt="Bar chart with two pairs of bars. Content-level hallucination: 42 percent without retrieval, 4 percent with retrieval. Citations grounded in a retrieved passage: 0 percent without retrieval, 51 to 89 percent with retrieval."}

Read the drop as structural, not as diligence. The same paper found the
*accuracy* gain from retrieval was large for weak models and small and not
statistically significant for strong ones, while the hallucination and
auditability gains were consistent across all of them [@pmid:42587692].
Grounding does not make a model smarter. It makes it *checkable*.

There is one more thing a grounded tool does that a general one cannot, and
you will produce it yourself in the Do block. Asked a question its sources do
not cover, a well-built grounded tool declines. A guideline chatbot for lung
cancer, asked about cancers the guideline did not cover, "consistently
declined to answer and indicated that the available information was
insufficient" [@pmid:42611847]. A general chatbot, asked the same question,
writes a paragraph. "I cannot find that in your sources" is the sentence that
tells you the tool is doing what it claims.

::: {.callout-note title="These numbers move"}
Every rate above is one tool, one domain, one month. The 2/1/0 study found the
ordering of the general chatbots differed between question types
[@pmid:42232526], and the overgeneralization study below found *newer* models
did worse than older ones [@pmid:40309181]. When your own run in the Do block
disagrees with a number here, that is expected. The pipeline in
@fig-rag-pipeline is the durable part.
:::

### The failure grounding does not fix

Go back to the opening answer. Its sources are real, its numbers are in Table
6, and its first sentence says retrieval "improved accuracy across all
models." The paper's own words are that the gain was "small and not
statistically significant for the already-strong bases." The answer's second
sentence half-corrects this, but the second sentence is not the one that goes
on the slide.

On the appraisal chapter's scale this is a **score 1**: a real reference, a
wrong characterization. It is also the most common kind of error a grounded
tool makes, and it is the kind that grounding, by construction, cannot catch.
The pipeline guarantees that the text came from the passages. It does not
guarantee that the model read the passages the way the authors meant them.
The dentistry study's phrasing is exact: the retrieval systems "avoided
fabricated references but still generated incorrect interpretations"
[@pmid:41266194].

The bias has a direction. When 10 widely used models were asked to summarize
scientific texts, most produced conclusions broader than the original even
when explicitly prompted for accuracy, some overgeneralizing in 26% to 73% of
cases, and model-written summaries were nearly five times more likely than
human-written ones to contain a broad generalization (odds ratio 4.85, 95% CI
3.06 to 7.70) [@pmid:40309181]. "In this subgroup" becomes "in patients."
"Was associated with" becomes "improves." "Not significant for the strong
models" becomes "across all models." The summary reads better than the paper,
which is exactly the problem.

::: {.callout-tip title="One real specimen, and how to catch it" collapse="true" #specimen}
**The run.** On 2026-09-07 the full text of Vollmer et al., *Diagnostics*
2026 [@pmid:42587692] was given to a source-grounded page summarizer (the
model behind the WebFetch tool in Claude Code, which the vendor does not name),
with the journal-club question in the opening scenario: *did adding retrieval
improve accuracy, and did it work for all the models?* The three-sentence
answer is reproduced verbatim at the top of this chapter. A second run on a
different paper in the same session [@pmid:42534267] produced a score-2
answer that correctly carried the authors' own caution about external
validation; the misreading is not inevitable, it is common.

**The check.** Click the citation on the first sentence. It lands on Table 6.
Two of the five confidence intervals cross zero. That is the whole check, and
it took less time than reading this paragraph. The general rule: for any
sentence you are going to repeat, click its citation and read *one line above
and one line below* the highlighted passage. The line below is where the
"however" lives.

**Before the cohort.** Re-run the same question in NotebookLM with the PMC
page as the source, record the model and date, and replace this specimen if
the live run gives a cleaner score 1. The point is not this tool; it is that
you can produce one yourself.
:::

### Three more things grounding cannot see

The pipeline answers from what you gave it. That produces three limits that no
citation link will reveal.

**The source set.** A confident summary of five weak papers is a confident
summary of five weak papers, with perfect citations. Grounding moves the
appraisal problem from the answer to the corpus: if you want to trust the
notebook, you have to trust what you put in it, and that is the appraisal
chapter's job.

**What is missing.** A notebook cannot cite a paper it does not contain, and
it will not tell you that the trial that would change your mind was published
last month and is not in your five PDFs. That is the difference between a
grounded search and a systematic one. The tool is excellent for *reading a
defined set of documents* and wrong for *what does the literature say*, where
the papers you failed to include are the ones that matter.

**Disagreement.** When two sources disagree, retrieval pulls passages from
both and generation writes one paragraph. The common behavior is to smooth
the disagreement into a consensus that no source holds. You will test this
directly in the Do block, with a pair of papers chosen because they disagree
about the same tool.

::: {.callout-important title="The practical rule"}
A grounded tool fixes the reference and helps with the attribution. It does
nothing for the claim. So: for any sentence you will repeat, click its
citation, read a line above and below, and ask whether the sentence is
narrower or broader than the passage. Broader is the usual direction. The
tool is a way of navigating sources, not a source; the citation in your slide
is the paper, which you have now read that part of.
:::

## Watch or listen

**Video.** IBM Technology, "What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?",
presented by Marina Danilevsky (23 August 2023; 6 min 36 s).
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T-D1OfcDW1M>

Six and a half minutes, no prerequisites, and the clearest whiteboard version
of @fig-rag-pipeline that exists. Listen for the anecdote about which planet
has the most moons: the speaker's confident wrong answer is the training-data
problem, and her fix, going to look it up, is retrieval. Then notice what the
video does not say. It presents retrieval as the answer to being wrong and
out of date. It never mentions that the model can retrieve the right passage
and misread it. That omission is the gap this chapter fills, and it is the
gap in every vendor's pitch you will hear.

**Reading alternative.** The written article this chapter is built on,
[Grounding AI in real sources](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-10-07-rag-notebooklm-idpt-8079/),
builds the context window from the World Series example and shows the
conversation as raw text. About fifteen minutes.

## Do

::: {.callout-warning title="No patient information, ever"}
Sources for this exercise are published papers, guidelines, or things you
wrote yourself. Not a de-identified case you typed up, not a screenshot of a
note, not your classmate's data. A consumer Google account carries no
business associate agreement, the contract that makes a vendor legally
responsible for protecting patient data, and an institutional account does not
change the rule unless your institution has said in writing that it does. The
line is bright on purpose, because the edge cases are where people get it
wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Getting in"}
NotebookLM is free with any Google account and runs in the browser. A
personal Gmail account works and asks for nothing beyond what you already gave
Google. If you sign in with your institutional Google account and NotebookLM
is missing or refuses to load, that is the school's administrator having
turned it off for your organizational unit, which they can do; do not spend
time on it, switch to a personal account. Google's own help page confirms that
most work and school accounts have access and that administrators control it
[VERIFY: institutional NotebookLM status at your school, the week before the cohort]{.verify}.

If you have no Google account and will not make one: your institutional
ChatGPT Edu or Copilot lets you attach files and say "answer only from the
attached documents." That gives you the same *exercise* with a weaker
*guarantee*, because a general chatbot instructed to stay in its sources will
still draw on its training when it wants to. Note in your write-up which tool
you used.
:::

### Step 1: choose your sources (10 minutes)

Pick three to five papers in your own specialty that you were already going
to read. If you do not have them, find them:

```
("large language model" OR "retrieval-augmented generation")
AND <your specialty> AND free full text[filter]
```

Filter PubMed to the last three years, read three abstracts, and take the
three to five papers that share a question. "Free full text" matters because
NotebookLM needs the paper, not the abstract: for each one, open the PMC
version and paste its URL as a website source, which is faster than
downloading and uploading the PDF and works the same way.

If you have no specialty yet, or want a set built to fail interestingly, use
this pre-vetted one. Every paper is open access on PMC, every one was verified
in PubMed on 2026-09-07, and they are deliberately about the tool you are
using:

| Paper | What it is | PMC |
|---|---|---|
| Vollmer et al., *Diagnostics* 2026 [@pmid:42587692] | Six models, 50 guideline questions, with and without retrieval | [PMC13465324](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13465324/) |
| Duran et al., *Digital Health* 2026 [@pmid:42534267] | NotebookLM for orthopedic disability rating: 91% vs 68% accuracy | [PMC13420063](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13420063/) |
| Seki et al., *Clinics and Practice* 2026 [@pmid:42645138] | NotebookLM classifying radiographs: agreement with dentists near zero | [PMC13511330](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13511330/) |
| Basu and Huynh, *BMC Health Serv Res* 2026 [@pmid:42251377] | Systematic review of 44 hallucination-mitigation studies | [PMC13470931](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13470931/) |

: A pre-vetted source set. Two of these papers disagree about whether NotebookLM is accurate, and they are both right. {#tbl-sources}

Make a new notebook, add the sources, and wait for each to finish processing.
That wait is steps 1 to 3 of @fig-rag-pipeline happening.

### Step 2: ask three questions and click every citation (10 minutes)

Ask three questions you would want answered for journal club. One of them
should be a question **you already know the answer to**, so you can judge the
answer rather than accept it. For the pre-vetted set, use these:

1. What did each paper measure, and what was its main result?
2. Did retrieval work for all the models in the guideline study?
3. Is NotebookLM accurate?

For every citation in every answer, not a sample, click it and read the
highlighted passage plus one line above and one line below. Score each
sentence-citation pair on the appraisal chapter's scale: **2** if the passage
supports the sentence as written, **1** if the passage is real but the
sentence is broader, narrower, or different, **0** if you cannot find support
in the passage at all. You are looking for a 1. There is usually at least one.

### Step 3: ask what the sources disagree about (5 minutes)

Ask a question your sources answer differently. For the pre-vetted set,
question 3 above is it: one paper found NotebookLM raised accuracy from 68%
to 91% on a guideline-bound rating task, another found its agreement with
dentists on radiographs was slight or worse. Watch what the tool does with
that. Does it present both, with the task each one measured? Or does it
produce a sentence like "NotebookLM shows promise but has limitations," which
is true of everything and cites both?

### Step 4: try to make it fabricate, then ask the chatbot (5 minutes)

Ask the notebook something its sources cannot support: a statistic that is
not in them, a named trial that is not there, a population none of the papers
studied. For the pre-vetted set: *What is the fabrication rate of NotebookLM
on citations in cardiology?* No source contains that. A grounded tool should
say so, hedge, or answer thinly.

Now ask the identical question in your general chatbot tab. Do not prompt it
carefully; ask it the way you asked the notebook. Compare on one axis only:
**can you verify where each sentence came from?** The chatbot's answer may be
better written and more useful. That is not the axis.

If your chatbot searched the web and cited pages, notice that this is a
different provenance question. The page is real; whether it is evidence is the
appraisal chapter's job.

### Record it

```
Tool: NotebookLM / other: ____________     Date: __________
Sources (3–5, with PMC IDs or titles):
  1 ______________________________________
  2 ______________________________________
  3 ______________________________________
  4 ______________________________________
  5 ______________________________________

Q1 ____________________________________  citations clicked ___  scores: 2s __ 1s __ 0s __
Q2 ____________________________________  citations clicked ___  scores: 2s __ 1s __ 0s __
Q3 ____________________________________  citations clicked ___  scores: 2s __ 1s __ 0s __

For the score-1 you found (or the closest to one): in one sentence, what did
the tool say, and what does the passage say?
________________________________________________________________________

Disagreement question: did the tool present both positions, or smooth them?
________________________________________________________________________

Fabrication attempt. What you asked: __________________________________
  Notebook said: ________________________________________________________
  Chatbot said:  ________________________________________________________
  Which one could you trace, sentence by sentence? _____________________
```

The score-1 sentence is your artifact. "Three of twelve citations were
stretched" is a number that will change next month; being able to say *how*
one was stretched is the skill.

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| The no-memory explanation | You can say what is re-sent each turn and why a new chat starts from zero, without the word "memory" | "It remembers the conversation" |
| The no-learning statement | You can say what changes between turns (the context) and what does not (the model), and separate that from where your text is stored | "It learns from what you type" |
| The pipeline | Six steps in order, and one sentence on what chunking does to a table | Fewer than six, or "it searches the documents" |
| The structural argument | You can say why a citation from a grounded tool points at a passage, and why that is not the same as the model being careful | "It's more accurate" |
| A scored set of citations | Every citation clicked; one score-1 sentence quoted beside its passage | Scores assigned by reading the answer alone |
| The disagreement result | You can say whether the tool presented both sources or smoothed them, and quote the smoothing sentence if it did | "It handled it fine" |
| The fabrication contrast | Both answers recorded; you can say which one you could trace and why the other reads better anyway | Only the notebook's answer |
| The search limit | You can say in one sentence when a grounded notebook is not a literature search | "It's good for research" |

## The standing question

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close this chapter. Two specifics. First, the next time a summary with
citations lands in front of you, from a notebook, an EHR tool, or a co-intern,
what is the one-minute check you will do before repeating a sentence from it,
and which of the failures in this chapter does that check catch? Second, go
back to Monday. The five PDFs are in the notebook, the first sentence of its
answer is on your draft slide, and journal club is Thursday. What do you
change on the slide, what do you say when the chief asks how you prepared,
and what do you do with the two papers that disagree? One word is not an
answer to either.

## Summary

- A chatbot has no memory. The conversation is re-sent every turn inside a
  fixed context window, and a new chat starts from zero.
- A model does not learn from you. The context changes; the model does not.
  Where your text is *stored* is a separate question, and the reason for the
  no-patient-information rule.
- Grounding is six steps: chunk, embed, index, retrieve, augment, generate.
  The model is handed passages and asked to paraphrase them.
- Chunking cuts on length, not meaning. A table split across two chunks is
  two real citations and no table.
- Grounded tools fabricate far less because a citation is a pointer to a
  passage in the window. That is structural, not diligence, and it is why the
  property generalizes to tools that do not exist yet.
- Grounding does not fix reading. A real, linked source can be misread, and
  the usual direction is broader than the paper. Click, read a line above and
  below, ask narrower or broader.
- A notebook answers from what you gave it. It is a way to read a defined set
  of documents, not a way to find out what the literature says.
- Thursday's slide: the number stays, the sentence changes, and the two
  papers that disagree get their own line each.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The overgeneralization study, 10 models and 4,900 summaries [@pmid:40309181].
  Its finding that newer models did worse is the "these numbers move" point
  applied to reading rather than references.
- The guideline-retrieval benchmark behind @fig-vollmer, with the transparent
  pipeline released openly [@pmid:42587692], and the systematic review of
  mitigation strategies that puts retrieval in context [@pmid:42251377].
- Two studies of NotebookLM itself, one where it helped [@pmid:42534267] and
  one where it was the wrong tool for an image task [@pmid:42645138]. Read
  them as a pair.
- The dentistry comparison whose phrase, "avoided fabricated references but
  still generated incorrect interpretations," is this chapter in nine words
  [@pmid:41266194].
- "Lost in the middle," the context-position experiment
  [@doi:10.1162/tacl_a_00638].
- A two-day workshop for clinicians that confines citation generation to
  NotebookLM and then makes participants verify every one; honest that whether
  this reduces fabrication was not tested [@pmid:42684317].

**Talks**

- [Grounding AI in real sources](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-10-07-rag-notebooklm-idpt-8079/):
  the written article this chapter is built on, with the conversation shown as
  raw text and the original shared-notebook exercise.
- [Word embeddings as the basis for LLMs](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-12-word-embeddings-basis-for-llms/):
  what "similar meaning, nearby numbers" actually means, with a hands-on
  embedding projector, for anyone who wants step 2 of the pipeline to stop
  being a black box.
- [Prompt engineering](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-17-prompt-engineering/):
  ten rules with clinical examples, for students whose Step 2 questions came
  back vague.
